Results Application of a PACE circuit for protease evolution To evolve proteases that cleave the cell death effectors procaspase-1 (Fig. 1a) and gasdermin D (Fig. 1b), we used a PACE circuit capable of reprogramming protease substrate specificity23. During positive selection, selection phage are modified to express the desired protease instead of gene III (gIII), a gene required for phage propagation35 (Fig. 1c). Host cells contain an accessory plasmid that encodes a protease-activated T7 RNA polymerase (RNAP), which transcribes gIII in response to protein cleavage, thereby linking phage propagation to protease activity. The T7 RNAP is fused to a catalytically disabled variant of T7 lysozyme, a natural inhibitor of T7 RNAP, via a cleavable linker containing the desired substrate. In the absence of protein cleavage, the high effective concentration of T7 lysozyme with respect to T7 RNAP ensures minimal RNAP activity. Cleavage liberates T7 lysozyme from being tethered to T7 RNAP, restoring RNAP activity. Selection stringency in PACE can be modulated by altering circuit parameters. For example, adjusting the ribosome binding site (RBS) strength48 upstream of gIII influences protein levels, while changing the promoter controlling expression of the RNAP–lysozyme fusion modulates the concentration of substrate available for proteolysis49. During negative selection (Fig. 1c), proteolysis liberates an orthogonal RNAP that expresses gIII-neg, a dominant-negative mutant of gIII50. The resulting gIII-neg impedes phage propagation by preventing detachment from the host membrane50. This dual-selection PACE circuit allows simultaneous selection for cleavage of a desired target protein and against cleavage of undesired off-target sequences.

Evolution of procaspase-1-cleaving proteases Our initial campaign targeted cleavage within the interdomain linker (IDL) of procaspase-1. Native procaspase-1 undergoes autoproteolytic cleavage at several positions within the IDL to promote activation5,51. We first established a starting point for evolution by comparing the IDL of procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) to a 17-amino-acid segment of the endogenous substrate of BoNT/X, vesicle-associated membrane protein 1 (VAMP1), positions 56–72. One alignment (Fig. 2a) placed the cleavage site of VAMP1 (between Arg 68 and Ala 69) at an autoproteolytic cleavage site of procaspase-1 (between Asp 316 and Ala 317). In this comparison, 14 of 17 residues recognized by BoNT/X protease differed between VAMP1 and procaspase-1, consistent with the lack of any apparent sequence similarity between these two proteins. Using this alignment, we identified a series of intermediate protein sequences to serve as evolutionary stepping-stones between VAMP1 and procaspase-1. We generally prioritize the most challenging specificity or activity changes early in the evolutionary process when the wild-type enzyme has the highest folding energy reserves to accommodate the impact of mutations that arise during evolution36. We found that the VAMP1-Asp70Ile mutation reduced cleavage by BoNT/X protease and was therefore selected as the first evolutionary stepping-stone (PC_SS1 hereafter; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2a–c). Having defined the initial evolutionary stepping-stone, we next implemented protease PACE positive selection to evolve BoNT/X toward procaspase-1 recognition (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1). PACE for 72 h on PC_SS1 evolved several mutations conserved among PACE clones: Thr167Ala, Pro174Leu and Ser240Asn (Supplementary Table 1). These mutations cluster near the BoNT/X protease substrate-binding groove, with Thr167Ala positioned close to the scissile bond. We characterized protease variants first with a luminescence reporter that uses the positive selection circuit to express luciferase from the T7

caspase-1 and gasdermin D. Gasdermins can be cleaved and activated by a diverse array of other proteases in addition to caspase-1, including hematopoietic cell proteases (for example, granzymes, neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G)17 and bacterial virulence factors (for example, SpeB)18. In this broader context, the presence of an active protease in the cytosol acts as an endogenous danger signal that triggers lytic cell death and immune responses. Ideally, such an approach would also be compatible with cell-type-specific delivery into cancer cells and would offer tunable specificities and pharmacokinetics to enable precise control of lytic cell death in therapeutic settings. Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) proteases19,20 are in widespread clinical use and could be promising starting points for such a strategy in light of their catalytic mechanism, modular architecture21, intrinsic ability to self-deliver into target cells22 and demonstrated evolvability23–25. BoNTs are dichain toxins composed of a light chain protease and a heavy chain, which is further divided into two functional domains: an N-terminal translocation domain (HN) and a C-terminal receptor-binding domain (HC)21. BoNTs have been approved for diverse indications, including cosmetic procedures, movement disorders, chronic migraines, autonomic dysfunctions and ophthalmological conditions, by inducing paralysis in various muscles26. The modular architecture of BoNTs makes them attractive targets for protein engineering; heavy chain and light chain domains can be swapped among serotypes27, additional cargos can be appended28–30, and receptor specificity can be enhanced by modifying the HC domain31. Prior work has shown that some wild-type BoNTs can induce apoptosis in certain cancer cells32,33, and targeted delivery using nanobody fusions to the HC have enhanced self-delivery selectivity for specific cancer cell types30. Despite these promising advances, BoNT proteases have not yet been engineered to directly induce changes in cell state such as the induction of lytic cell death. Recent developments in phage-assisted continuous evolution (PACE)34 have substantially expanded our ability to generate bespoke proteases23,35,36, yielding evolved BoNT proteases that selectively cleave target proteins other than their native SNARE substrates23. Although PACE can select against the cleavage of researcherdefined off-target substrates, it does not explicitly select against the cleavage of other off-target proteins that an evolving protease may acquire the ability to process during evolution. Traditional proteomics-based methods, such as N-terminomics37–39 and proteomic identification of protease cleavage sites40, are well suited for global analyses of protease activity but can be low throughput and may lack the sensitivity to detect low-frequency, yet biologically perturbative, off-target cleavage events. Display technologies enable high-throughput screening of diverse randomized peptide libraries41 and human-proteome-derived libraries42,43 but typically require purified protease, which can pose challenges for unstable or difficult-to-express protease variants. We developed a sensitive, high-throughput, scalable system for profiling the cleavage activity of natural and evolved BoNT proteases on thousands of substrates simultaneously by adapting the genetic circuitry of PACE into a pooled activity-enrichment assay. Here we expand the functional repertoire of BoNTs by applying PACE to evolve BoNT serotype X (BoNT/X) proteases44–47 that cleave and activate procaspase-1 or gasdermin D. Targeting two key mediators of inflammatory cell death provides a strategy to modulate cancer cell fate. Using our substrate profiling method, we showed that the evolved proteases exhibit a highly altered cleavage profile compared to the starting wild-type BoNT/X protease. Next, we evaluated the proteases in cancer cells and demonstrated that the gasdermin D-cleaving variant induced lytic cell death in several cancer cell lines. Interestingly, the procaspase-1-cleaving protease triggered concurrent lytic and apoptotic cell death across multiple cancer types. Although Thr167Ala, Pro174Leu and Ser240Asn mutations were retained during PANCE on PC_SS2, additional conserved mutations emerged, including Asn144Ile, Ala218Val and Tyr314Ser (Supplementary Table 1). Variants such as X(SS2)a, X(SS2)c, X(SS2)f and X(SS2)g exhibited moderate activity on PC_SS2 while retaining activity on VAMP1 and PC_SS1, with no detected activity on procaspase-1 in the luminescence assay (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). These results suggest that even though PANCE on PC_SS2 yielded active proteases, and PC_SS2 shares >50% homology with procaspase-1, additional evolution is necessary to evolve activity on the procaspase-1 substrate. Subsequent evolution campaigns selected directly for cleavage of procaspase-1 (residues 304–320; Fig. 2a,b). First, PANCE on a low-stringency positive selection circuit yielded proteases X(PC1)c, X(PC1)d and X(PC1)e, which showed weak activity on procaspase-1 and residual activity on VAMP1, PC_SS1 and PC_SS2 (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). To increase activity, we transitioned to PACE using a more stringent circuit, replacing the T7 RNAP promoter with the weaker T3′ RNAP promoter50 and adjusting RBS strength in front of gIII to reduce transcriptional activation following RNAP liberation (Extended Data Fig. 1). To accommodate these adjustments, the 17-residue procaspase-1 substrate was placed in the linker between T3′ RNAP and the inhibitor T7 lysozyme; while the T3′ RNAP variant has high selectivity for the T3 promoter, it remains effectively inhibited by T7 lysozyme23. After several passages, protease variants X(PC2)a–X(PC2)e demonstrated substantial activity on procaspase-1 (Fig. 2c), with enriched mutations such as Asp161Asn, Asn164Lys, Asn235Ile, Ser279Pro and Ser280Pro likely contributing to this gain (Supplementary Table 1). Residual activity on VAMP1 (residues 28–88), however, highlighted the need for negative selection (Extended Data Fig. 2c). Phage surviving procaspase-1 positive selection PACE were therefore subjected to dual-selection PACE, incorporating positive selection for procaspase-1 and negative selection against VAMP1. Proteases emerging from the first round of dual selection, including X(PC3)a and X(PC3)c, showed decreased activity on VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In a second round of dual selection, proteases were evolved under a more stringent selection that lowered the amount of available positive selection substrate and increased the concentration of gIII-neg (Extended Data Fig. 1). Resulting variants, X(PC4)a–X(PC4)d, were less active on procaspase-1 than X(PC2) and X(PC3) proteases, but were highly selective for procaspase-1 cleavage (Fig. 2c), losing all detected activity on VAMP1 and PC_ SS1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Overall, these findings indicate that phage-assisted evolution successfully reprogrammed wild-type BoNT/X to cleave procaspase-1 while eliminating any detected activity on its native substrate VAMP1.

In vitro characterization of procaspase-1-cleaving proteases We selected X(PC4)c, hereafter referred to as X(PC), from the final round of dual-selection PACE for detailed analysis due to its robust expression and ease of purification (see Fig. 2d for sequence). We compared the activity of wild-type BoNT/X and X(PC) on fusion proteins containing the targeted regions of either procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) or VAMP1 (residues 28–88), inserted between maltose-binding protein (MBP) and glutathione S-transferase (GST) proteins to facilitate bacterial expression and purification of these substrates. As expected, wild-type BoNT/X cleaved the VAMP1 fusion but showed no detectable activity on the procaspase-1 substrate (Extended Data Fig. 3a). By contrast, X(PC) selectively cleaved the procaspase-1 substrate with no activity on VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 3a). These data confirm that X(PC) retains selective activity on procaspase-1 and has lost its ability to cleave its native substrate when tested in purified protein assays. We quantified the kinetic parameters of X(PC) to validate the selectivity suggested by luciferase activity and assess how evolution impacted catalytic efficiency. Using a previously reported fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based assay23 (Fig. 2e,f), we determined that X(PC) cleaving procaspase-1 has a Km of 4.05 µM, a kcat of 0.423 s−1 and a kcat/Km (catalytic efficiency) of 0.104 s−1 µM−1. Despite undergoing negative selection only on VAMP1, X(PC) also lost activity on all other known native BoNT/X substrates, including VAMP4, VAMP5 and YKT6 (Fig. 2e). Using the same FRET-based assay, we compared the activity of X(PC) to that of wild-type BoNT/X protease on its native substrate VAMP1 (Km = 6.93 µM, kcat = 3.52 s−1, kcat / Km = 0.508 s−1 µM−1; Fig. 2e,f). X(PC) on procaspase-1 is only fivefold slower than wild-type BoNT/X protease on VAMP1. These findings highlight that PACE can reprogram substrate specificity with high selectivity, rather than merely broaden protease promiscuity. We previously observed that BoNT proteases can evolve to cleave a target substrate at a peptide bond that differs from the anticipated cleavage site23. Indeed, mass spectrometry revealed that cleavage by X(PC) occurred between Glu 314 and Asp 315 rather than the predicted site between Asp 316 and Ala 317 inferred from its alignment with VAMP1 (Fig. 2a). Luminescence-based activity assays suggest that this cleavage site shift evolved during higher-stringency rounds of selection on procaspase-1. Early variants from low-stringency selection on procaspase-1 (X(PC1)a–X(PC1)c) showed little activity on procaspase-1 but retained activity on PC_SS1 and VAMP1. By contrast, variants from higher-stringency campaigns (X(PC2)a–X(PC2)e) evolved strong activity on procaspase-1, maintained activity on VAMP1 but lost activity on PC_SS1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). These observations suggest that as stringency increased, evolving proteases selected for a P2′ aspartic acid preference, a feature present at the observed cleavage sites in both VAMP1 and procaspase-1, but absent in PC_SS1 (Fig. 2a).

Characterization of procaspase-1 cleavage in mammalian cells To determine whether X(PC) can cleave full-length procaspase-1 in a cellular context, we transfected hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged procaspase-1-Cys285Ala into HEK293T cells and incubated lysates with decreasing doses of purified proteases (Extended Data Fig. 3b). The Cys285Ala substitution renders procaspase-1 catalytically inactive, preventing toxicity in HEK293T cells. Whereas BoNT/X showed no activity, X(PC) cleaved procaspase-1-Cys285Ala (Extended Data Fig. 3b). These findings demonstrate that X(PC) can cleave full-length procaspase-1 in protein lysates even though it was evolved on only a 17-amino-acid substrate fragment, procaspase-1 (residues 304–320). Next, we determined if X(PC) remains functional when expressed intracellularly in mammalian cells. HEK293T cells were co-transfected with HA-tagged X(PC) and Flag-tagged procaspase-1-Cys285Ala, and protease activity was assessed by immunoblotting (Fig. 2g). In cells expressing procaspase-1-Cys285Ala, X(PC) generated a distinct cleavage product at the expected molecular weight corresponding to procaspase-1 cleavage. Together, these results demonstrate that X(PC) remains catalytically active when expressed in mammalian cells and can cleave full-length procaspase-1 even in the presence of the endogenous intracellular human proteome.

Evolving procaspase-1-cleaving proteases with reduced off-target cleavage activity Although X(PC) demonstrated high selectivity for procaspase-1 over VAMP1, its transfection into mammalian cells lacking procaspase-1 (HEK293T cells) still resulted in reduced cell viability compared to a catalytically inactive X(PC) variant, consistent with residual off-target activity (Extended Data Fig. 3c). To determine how this off-target activity may have changed during directed evolution, we transfected wild-type BoNT/X protease at the same concentration. Notably, BoNT/X was approximately tenfold more toxic than X(PC) in this cell line, as measured by CellTiter-Glo assay 48 h after transfection (Extended Data Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 1). While this toxicity may reflect the promiscuity of BoNT/X compared to other serotypes, it is also possible that BoNT/X cleaves an unidentified host protein essential to HEK293T survival44,45. To understand the nature of X(PC)’s off-target cleavage activity more deeply, we began by investigating cleavage of downstream caspase-1 substrates and observed that X(PC) likely cleaved IL-1β (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 3d,e) at a position distinct from caspase-1 cleavage events following Asp 26 and Asp 116. Based on a sequence alignment between procaspase-1 and IL-1β (Fig. 2a), and observed cleavage product sizes (Fig. 2h), we hypothesized that X(PC) cleaves IL-1β in the flexible N-terminal region of the protein between Glu 18 and Asp 19. We also identified ORC1 based on P2–P4′ homology to procaspase-1 (Extended Data Fig. 2b) and noted that evolved variants also cleaved ORC1 (residues 691–707) in the luminescence assay (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Thus, although negative selection against VAMP1 reduces cleavage on SNARE targets, evolution on procaspase-1 appears to confer caspase-like substrate preferences

that include IL-1β or substrates with complete homology to the P2–P4′ of procaspase-1 such as ORC1 (residues 691–707). As this region of ORC1 cleaved by X(PC4) variants occurs in a section of the protein predicted to be structured and therefore may be less accessible to a protease, we prioritized eliminating cleavage of IL-1β by performing evolution using dual-selection PANCE with a 25-amino-acid segment from IL-1β as the negative selection substrate, IL-1β (residues 5–29; Fig. 2a). Variants X(PC5)a–X(PC5)c emerged with mutations, including a shift of Thr167Ala to Thr167Ser (Supplementary Table 1). In luminescence activity profiling, these variants retained comparable activity on the procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) substrate used for evolution as X(PC), but showed no cleavage of IL-1β (residues 5–29) or ORC1 (residues 691–707; Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2b–g). These results confirm that dual-selection strategies can further reduce off-target cleavage while maintaining desired target cleavage activity within the PACE environment. We next tested the ability of X(PC5) variants to cleave full-length proteins in HEK293T cells by co-transfecting plasmids expressing either procaspase-1-Cys285Ala or IL-1β, along with evolved proteases (Fig. 2g). Variants X(PC5)a and X(PC5)b showed partial cleavage of full-length procaspase-1, whereas X(PC5)c showed no detectable activity. Cleavage of full-length IL-1β was not detected in all three cases (Fig. 2h). While these results demonstrate that further negative selection reduced off-target cleavage, all three variants performed worse than X(PC) at cleaving full-length procaspase-1 in mammalian cells. Western blots suggest that the reduced cleavage by X(PC5) variants likely stems from lower expression and stability of the proteases in mammalian cells (Fig. 2g).

Substrate specificity profiling of natural and evolved proteases To assess the substrate preferences of a protease in a broad and rapid manner, we developed a method for profiling protease activity on a substrate library by adapting the PACE selection circuit. We reasoned that replacing the T7 RNAP-transcribed gIII cassette with a chloramphenicol resistance gene would enable the selective enrichment of bacterial cells that express substrates cleaved by a protease of interest when challenged with antibiotic (Fig. 3a). We could express a protease of interest under an inducible promoter and select in the presence of chloramphenicol in Escherichia coli expressing a large library of peptide substrates present in the linker between T7 RNAP and its fused T7 lysozyme inhibitor. The DNA sequence encoding cleaved peptides could be identified by high-throughput sequencing of library members in surviving bacteria to quantify the relative activity of the protease on all substrates in the library via high-throughput sequencing. Validation experiments established that cells expressing T7 RNAP–linker–T7 lysozyme fusions containing various substrate sequences exhibited growth rates in the presence of chloramphenicol that correlate with the protease’s known activity on that substrate (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b), demonstrating the potential of this strategy to serve as a protease substrate profiling method. As an initial application of the method, we generated a library of all possible single-residue substitutions to a 60-mer VAMP1 sequence and assessed the cleavage activities of wild-type BoNT/X and BoNT/F proteases on this library (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 2c–f). We found that BoNT/X exhibits a substantially greater tolerance for substitutions in the native substrate sequence than BoNT/F. BoNT/X protease cleaves VAMP1 between Arg 68 and Ala 69, and notable de-enrichment at Ala 69 and Asp 70, along with slight de-enrichment at Arg 68 in the substrate profile, suggests that P1, P1′ and P2′ primarily dictate BoNT/X protease substrate recognition (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4a). The protease appears particularly selective at the P1′ position, tolerating only cysteine, glycine, serine or the wild-type residue alanine. Notably, the P11 position, corresponding to Arg 58 in VAMP1, slightly de-enriches most amino acids aside from arginine, suggesting that P11 may participate in an important exosite contact (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Beyond these key positions, BoNT/X protease exhibits tolerance to mutations, which may contribute to its broad SNARE substrate range44,45. By contrast, BoNT/F light chain, when profiled on VAMP1 (Supplementary Fig. 2c), exhibited greater selectivity. BoNT/F protease cleaves between Gln 60 and Lys 61, with stringent amino acid preferences at multiple positions surrounding the cleavage site. These findings are consistent with previous reports that BoNT/F light chain cleaves only VAMP1, VAMP2 and VAMP3, while BoNT/X cleaves VAMP1 through VAMP5 as well as YKT6 (refs. 44,45). These findings also support our observation that BoNT/X protease causes toxicity in HEK293T cells, likely due to cleavage of additional, unidentified substrates (Supplementary Fig. 1). After confirming that X(PC)’s activity in the selection circuit correlates with its to luminescence-detected protease activity (Supplementary Fig. 3a), we performed a similar analysis on proteases evolved to cleave procaspase-1 using a library of all possible single-residue substitutions of a 17-mer substrate sequence (Fig. 3a). Compared to wild-type BoNT/X protease, both X(PC2)b, an earlier evolutionary intermediate with activity on both VAMP1 and procaspase-1, and X(PC) demonstrated more stringent substrate requirements (Fig. 3b,c and Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). X(PC), which cleaves procaspase-1 between Glu 314 and Asp 315, displayed strict specificity at positions P3, P2, P1, P1′, P2′ and P3′ (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 3e). Next, we sought to identify combinations of substitutions in the procaspase-1 substrate that could be cleaved by our evolved proteases. X(PC) shows selectivity for residues at six amino acids within the procaspase-1 substrate sequence from P3 to P3′ (Fig. 3c). Testing all possible combinations of these residues would require a library of 109 sequences, above the limits of our high-throughput sequencing readout. We therefore sought a strategy to reduce the scale of the library to remain within the quantitative throughput limits of our assay (up to ~40,000 substrates), while still assaying a full repertoire of sequences likely to be cleaved by our evolved proteases (Extended Data Fig. 4b). We observed that wild-type BoNT/X displays co-linearities on second-order combinations of substrate residue substitutions; that is, cleavage activity on single-residue substitutions is predictive of cleavage activity on combinations of those substitutions (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Given this observation, we reasoned that testing X(PC) on a library of residue combinations for which each single-residue substitution shows activity would have high predictive power for identifying sequences cleaved by the protease. For substrate positions that are broadly tolerant of all single-residue substitutions, we retained the procaspase-1 residue. We assessed the cleavage activity of X(PC) on this library of 2,880 high-activity substrates (Extended Data Fig. 4b). The cleavage profile we observed for the protease was consistent with our observations of X(PC) in vitro cleavage, with procaspase-1 enriching in the top 97.8% of substrates (log2 (fold enrichment) = 2.68) and IL-1β enriching in

the top 83.5% of substrates (log2 (fold enrichment) = 1.05; Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). We also observed that mean enrichment of a substrate decreases monotonically with increasing Hamming distance to procaspase-1, consistent with our hypothesis that cleavage activity on single-residue substitutions is predictive of cleavage activity on higher-order combinations of substitutions (Supplementary Fig. 4b). To identify potential off-target substrates, we searched enriched motifs against the human proteome, using the enrichment score of the IL-1β motif (cleavage between Glu 18 and Asp 19) as the cutoff for predicted cleavage activity (Fig. 3d). Candidate hits could be categorized in multiple ways, such as by sorting for flexible regions or restricting expression by cell types. To prioritize biologically relevant candidates and based on our hypothesis that the evolved protease favors caspase substrates, we cross-referenced the hits with the MerCASBA database56 of known caspase substrates, identifying potential cleavage events associated with cell death. This analysis revealed 294 shared substrates, 34 of which, including caspase-1, were predicted to be cleaved by X(PC) within 30 amino acids of a caspase cleavage site and in a flexible region, as determined by AlphaFold structural models (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Flexible regions containing both caspase and predicted X(PC) cleavage sites in these 34 candidate substrates were cloned into a T7 RNAP–lysozyme fusion construct (Extended Data Fig. 4c) and evaluated using luminescence-based activity profiling (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Five substrates did not express well in the PACE circuit and were excluded from further analysis. X(PC) showed positive activity on 11 substrates. Among these, five (claspin (CLSPN), catenin β-1 (CTNB1), eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 subunit J (EIF3J), DNA replication licensing factor MCM5 (MCM5) and transcription factor p65 (TF65)) exhibited X(PC)-dependent activity at least 50,000 over background. These substrates play key roles in cell survival processes, including cell cycle checkpoints (CLSPN), Wnt signaling (CTNB1), DNA replication (MCM5), protein synthesis (EIF3J) and transcriptional regulation of immune and inflammatory responses (TF65). Thus, X(PC)-mediated cleavage near caspase sites in these proteins may contribute to the complex, multipathway cell death characterized in subsequent cellular assays. We further validated the nominated substrates by expressing full-length proteins in HEK293T cells and incubating lysate with 1 µM X(PC) and BoNT/X protease (Extended Data Fig. 4e). X(PC), but not BoNT/X protease, cleaved full-length coatomer subunit alpha (COPα), desmoglein-3 (DSG3), Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor 2 (ARHG2), TF65, EIF3J, and CLSPN. Regarding the identification of off-target substrates, higher enrichment scores generally correlated with protease activity on the flexible substrate, as measured by luminescence. For example, 70% of substrates with a log2 (fold enrichment) greater than 2.0 generated a luminescent signal (Extended Data Fig. 4d), and four of five substrates with the highest luminescence values had enrichment scores above 2.0 (CLSPN = 3.526, EIF3J = 2.219, MCM5 = 2.125 and TF65 = 4.204). Conversely, only 29% of substrates with enrichment values below 2.0 produced a detectable signal (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Luminescence values and enrichment scores were also reasonable predictors of full-length substrate cleavage activity: of the seven substrates that were cleaved, all but one ranked in the top 50th percentile of enrichment scores (Fig. 3d), and four of five substrates with luminescence values over 50,000 were cleaved in full-length format (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Overall, these findings demonstrate that this substrate profiling system can both predict and validate physiologically relevant off-target cleavage events, thereby providing critical information for refining protease specificity for intended applications.

(TMT-TAILs). This technique uses isotopic labeling of primary amines following X(PC) proteolysis and subsequent negative selection of trypsin-generated internal peptides to enrich for neo-N termini57. We first used HEK293T cells, which lack endogenous caspase-1, to identify off-target cleavage events against a clean background (Extended Data Fig. 5a). High-confidence substrates were identified by filtering for TMT-labeled neo-N termini significantly enriched in cells treated with active proteases compared to cells not treated with a protease or those treated with a catalytically inactive ‘dead’ control. This analysis identified six primary substrates—peroxiredoxin-4 (PRDX4), GRB10-interacting GYF protein 2 (GGYF2), ubiquitin-like-conjugating enzyme ATG3 (ATG3), RNA-binding protein 33 (RBM33), heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K (HNRPK) and galactokinase (GALK1)—with a greater than one log2 fold change (log2FC) enrichment (P < 0.05), along with three additional candidates that approached this threshold: calumenin (CALU), 60-kDa heat shock protein (CH60), mitochondrial and tubulin α-3D chain(TUBA3D) (Fig. 3e). We validated these candidate substrates by incubating X(PC) with lysates expressing MYC-tagged variants or with recombinant MBP–substrate–GST fusion reporters. X(PC), but not wild-type BoNT/X, cleaved all nine candidates at sizes consistent with the cleavage sites predicted by TMT-TAILs peptides (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Mass spectrometry revealed the exact peptide bond cleaved in GRB10-interacting GYF protein 2 and RNA-binding protein 33. Notably, 60-kDa heat shock protein, mitochondrial and TUBA3D, and GRB10-interacting GYF protein 2 were also identified in our bacterial substrate profiling method. While we did not confirm if cleavage of these substrates activates cell death, we hypothesize they may accelerate cell death via inflammatory or apoptotic pathways. For example, ubiquitin-like-conjugating enzyme ATG3 cleavage by caspase-8 accelerates apoptosis58, heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K is a known caspase-3 substrate59, and peroxiredoxin-4 limits caspase-1 activation60. We next sought to establish caspase-1 cleavage as a positive control for the TMT-TAILS pipeline. Because trypsin generates a difficult-to-detect caspase-1 peptide through successive cleavage, we switched to chymotrypsin and tracked target cleavage using either an MBP–caspase-1–GST fusion spiked into HEK293T cell lysates or endogenous caspase-1 in SUP-B15 cells. Filtering for TMT-labeled N termini identified tubulin α-1B chain as the top hit in HEK293T cells with a threefold enrichment (P = 0.04; Extended Data Fig. 5d). Tubulin-β, protein disulfide-isomerase A3 and S-methyl-5′-thioadenosine phosphorylase also appeared as significant hits (L2FC > 1, P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 5d). In SUP-B15 cells, protein disulfide-isomerase A3 was the primary hit, and, while tubulin α-1B chain was similarly enriched (L2FC > 1), it did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.22; Extended Data Fig. 5e). The identification of tubulins and protein disulfide-isomerase A3 across both cell lines suggests that X(PC) may promote cell death by targeting structural and apoptotic regulatory proteins, thereby mimicking broad caspase proteolysis activity during programmed cell death. Although direct neo-N-terminal fragments of caspase-1 were not enriched in the TMT-TAILS dataset, potentially due to labeling inefficiencies, we observed significant depletion of peptides spanning the X(PC) cleavage site in the active protease-treated samples, providing strong evidence of on-target cleavage (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Collectively, these results validate TMT-TAILs as an effective strategy for off-target substrate nomination and suggest that X(PC) induces a multipathway cell death response by cleaving endogenous caspase targets across both apoptotic and inflammatory pathways.

Evolution of gasdermin D-cleaving proteases BoNT/X protease was also used as a starting point for the evolution of proteases targeting the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (Fig. 1b). Similar to the procaspase-1 evolution, 17 amino acids from the gasdermin D IDL (residues 257–273) were used to generate an alignment

that maintained homology at positions Leu 263, Ser 264 and Leu 273 compared to VAMP1 (Fig. 4a). Two single-point mutant stepping-stones were selected based on their ability to decrease BoNT/X protease activity: stepping-stone 1.1, GD_SS1.1, with an arginine>leucine substitution at the P1 position, and stepping-stone 1.2, GD_SS1.2, with an aspartic acid>asparagine substitution at P2′. After 11 PANCE passages of parallel evolution on GD_SS1.1 and GD_SS1.2, isolated proteases revealed consensus mutations at Asp29Asn, Asn143Asp and Pro174Leu (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 2). Although Asp29Asn was unique to GD_SS1.2 evolution, Asn143Asp and Pro174Leu were present in both trajectories and likely contributed to increased substrate flexibility. This hypothesis was supported by luminescence activity data, which showed that all profiled variants had activity on both GD_SS1.1 and GD_SS1.2, regardless of their evolutionary trajectory (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). The outputs from GD_SS1.1 and GD_SS1.2 were pooled and evolved using PANCE on the second stepping-stone, GD_SS2, a substrate containing five additional substitutions from gasdermin D (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6). Evolved variants displayed activity on GD_SS2 (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Next, outputs from GD_SS2 were pooled and directly evolved on GD_Sh, the 17-amino-acid region from the gasdermin D IDL (Pro 257– Leu 273). Output proteases X(GD_Sh1)a and X(GD_Sh1)c exhibited activity on GD_Sh (Extended Data Fig. 7d), but retained activity on earlier substrates, necessitating the introduction of negative selection. The first dual-selection PANCE (GD_Sh2) used GD_Sh as the positive selection substrate and VAMP1 as the negative selection substrate. Low-stringency negative selection (Extended Data Fig. 6) yielded outputs X(GD_Sh2)a and X(GD_Sh2)b that retained activity on GD_SS1.1, GD_SS1.2 and GD_SS2, indicating that further selection was necessary (Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). To increase selection stringency, the RBS strength in front of gIII-neg was gradually enhanced over the subsequent PANCE passages (Extended Data Fig. 6). Concerned about the possibility of proteases evolving to cleave within the T7 lysozyme or linker regions, we introduced a null negative selection construct during the final passages to remove proteases that cleaved outside of the target. In this construct, the target cleavage sequence was entirely omitted, leaving T7 lysozyme fused directly to T7 RNAP via the standard GGS linker (Extended Data Fig. 6). Isolated proteases X(GD_Sh2)c and X(GD_Sh2)d retained activity on GD_Sh, but lost activity on GD_SS1.1, GD_SS1.2 and GD_SS2 (Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). Despite their activity on GD_Sh, evolved proteases failed to cleave longer gasdermin D IDL sequences in luminescence assays (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7e). This result suggested they might be recognizing nontarget features, such as the GGS linker between lysozyme and RNAP, rather than authentic substrate residues. In vitro cleavage assays using either the GD_Sh substrate (Pro 257–Leu 273) or a 41-amino-acid fragment of gasdermin D (Ala 244–Thr 284; GD_M) fused between MBP and GST showed no detectable cleavage by X(GD_Sh2)c (Extended Data Fig. 8a). These results suggest that longer, more native substrates were required to guide specificity toward native gasdermin D cleavage. We therefore initiated selection on a longer gasdermin D substrate, GD_M (Ala 244–Thr 284), using truncated GGS linkers to minimize the opportunity for the evolution of linker recognition. We initiated an evolution campaign with seven PANCE passages on GD_M, followed by 12 passages of high-stringency dual selection penalizing proteases that cleave VAMP1, and concluded with 16 passages on a circuit using a weaker promoter in front of the GD_M substrate to increase positive selection stringency (Extended Data Fig. 6). Variants X(GD_M1)b and X(GD_M1)c acquired mutations (Ala73Ser, Ala163Thr, Lys193Arg, Phe244Leu and Glu266Asp; Supplementary Table 2) and showed improved luminescence activity on GD_M and GD_Sh (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e). These results indicated that BoNT/X evolution was continuing toward improved recognition of authentic gasdermin D substrates.

To further enhance catalytic performance, phage pools of proteases surviving PANCE on GD_M were combined and evolved in two successive PACE campaigns. The first (GD_M2) involved 125 h of lower-stringency dual selection, followed by 85 h of high-stringency evolution. Isolated variants X(GD_M2)a–X(GD_M2)c showed improved luminescence-based activity on GD_M (Extended Data Fig. 7e). A second PACE (GD_M3) extended this evolution by an additional 184 h using the same high-stringency circuit. Enriched mutations from earlier rounds were retained (Supplementary Table 2). Although in vitro cleavage of GD_M by GD_M2a improved (Extended Data Fig. 8a), performance still lagged behind earlier evolved BoNT proteases. This observation suggested that further refinements in the circuit design or selection conditions were needed. Two final PACE campaigns were conducted to optimize specificity and activity. In GD_M4, a synthetic RBS was introduced to reduce translation of gIII, thereby increasing the stringency of selection for proteases that produce higher RNAP output (Extended Data Fig. 6). In the final round of PACE, we increased the evolution substrate to a longer 65-residue region, GD_L (Val 222–Asp 286), to better reflect the native IDL context. Proteases from these rounds (X(GD_M4)b, X(GD_M4)c, X(GD_L)a and X(GD_L)c) showed enhanced in vitro cleavage of MBP– GST GD_M with no detected activity on VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 8b,c). Together, these results demonstrate that reprogramming BoNT/X protease to cleave gasdermin D is achievable through iterative substrate design, negative selection and circuit optimization.

Engineering of gasdermin D-cleaving proteases Although the evolved X(GD_L) proteases displayed promising activity through profiling activity in the PACE architecture, they failed to yield measurable kinetic parameters or substrate cleavage in mammalian cells, likely due to insufficient catalytic activity (Fig. 4c,d). To enhance performance, we selected variants X(GD_M4)c, X(GD_L)a, X(GD_L) b and X(GD_L)c for reversion testing (Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). The effects of the reversions were evaluated by measuring GD_M substrate cleavage using either a GD_M sequence fused between MBP and GST (Supplementary Fig. 5a) or using a FRET-based substrate (Supplementary Fig. 5b). Some reversions, such as Arg242Tyr and Phe244Leu, substantially reduced activity on GD_M, whereas others, particularly in regions spanning residues 1–67 and 314–439, maintained or improved activity (Supplementary Fig. 5a,b and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). These results indicate that many mutations acquired during early rounds of PANCE and dual selection were not essential for gasdermin D cleavage and, in some cases, were detrimental to protease efficiency in the context of GD_L variants. As an alternative approach to increasing protease activity, we pooled all X(PC4) output phage from the successful high-stringency, dual-selection PACE on procaspase-1 with negative selection on VAMP1 and evolved them on the GD_M substrate. One resulting mutation, Glu72Arg, emerged as especially promising because it lies near the scissile bond (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). Introduction of this mutation, along with reversions in previously described regions, into X(GD_L)a, X(GD_L)b and X(GD_L)c led to detectable FRET activity. For example, variant X(GD_L)c.3 (later renamed X(GD_L)f) had a catalytic efficiency of 0.004 µM−1 s−1, whereas the parent X(GD_L)c that lacked reversion and engineering showed no detectable activity on the FRET substrate (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Similar trends were observed with X(GD_L)a and X(GD_L)b reversion/engineered variants (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Accordingly, we combined the most effective reversion positions with Glu72Arg and applied them to the X(GD_L) a–X(GD_L)c background to generate X(GD_L)d–X(GD_L)f (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 2). Despite the kinetic gains, proteases still lacked cleavage activity in mammalian cells and suffered from poor expression (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 5d). Encouraged by the gain-of-function from Glu72Arg, we searched for additional mutations enriched during the evolution of X(PC4)

phages on the GD_M substrate (Supplementary Table 5) with the goal of improving activity so that proteolysis would be detectable in mammalian cells. Among the mutations considered, Glu113Lys enhanced catalytic performance and was added to X(GD_L)d–X(GD_L)f to yield X(GD_L)g–X(GD_L)i. The best-performing variant, X(GD_L)i, hereafter referred to as X(GD) (sequence listed in Fig. 4e), exhibited a catalytic efficiency of 0.013 µM−1 s−1 (Fig. 4c) and improved cleavage of the GST– gasdermin D substrate in mammalian cells, indicating enhanced protease activity (Fig. 4d). This mutation also increased expression of the protease in mammalian cells, restoring it to levels near that of wild-type BoNT/X protease (Fig. 4d). This progressive grafting strategy highlights the additivity of evolved mutations and illustrates how rational recombination of beneficial substitutions can fine-tune substrate specificity and activity.

Substrate profiling gasdermin D-cleaving proteases We applied our substrate profiling method using a positional scanning library based on the GD_M substrate with a few optimizations to the T7 substrate profiling plasmid (Supplementary Fig. 6). We first profiled X(GD) (Extended Data Fig. 8d) and its immediate precursor in the engineering campaign, X(GD_L)f (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Fig. 7a). Although X(GD_L)f is 3.3-fold less catalytically efficient than X(GD), the substrate specificity profiles of the two proteases were highly similar. Overall, both X(GD_L)f and X(GD) exhibit more stringent substrate requirements than wild-type BoNT/X protease or X(PC). For example, X(GD_L)f and X(GD) show strong preferences at positions P12, P7, P6, P4–P1, P1′ and P2′. According to the X(GD) enrichment profile (Extended Data Fig. 8d), positions P12, P3 and P1′ show positive enrichment only for the amino acid found at that position in native gasdermin D. Additionally, P7 and P2′ show positive enrichment for only one alternative amino acid besides the native residue. These results suggest that although the X(GD_L) proteases, including X(GD), are less catalytically active than wild-type BoNT/X protease and X(PC), they are more selective. Profiling the gasdermin D-targeting proteases also illuminated why variants evolved on GD_Sh were able to pass PACE selection but failed to cleave longer gasdermin D substrates in vitro. For example, X(GD_Sh2)c exhibits considerable luminescence activity on GD_Sh when the substrate is fused between lysozyme and T7 RNAP (Extended Data Fig. 7d), but shows no detectable cleavage when the same substrate is fused between MBP and GST and tested in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Profiling X(GD_Sh2)c on a positional scan of GD_M revealed a strong preference for an arginine near the N-terminus of the substrate (Supplementary Fig. 7b,c). This preference resembles that of wild-type BoNT/X, which prefers an arginine at the P11 position in VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 4a). In the PACE substrate architecture, X(GD_Sh2)c cleavage may have been facilitated by an arginine residue within lysozyme located 11 positions upstream of the first proline in the GD_Sh sequence. While X(GD_Sh2)c’s exact cleavage site remains unconfirmed, both this P1 proline and P12 arginine are established substrate positions for the later X(GD_L)f and X(GD) variants. Thus, substrate profiling not only revealed the increased specificity of X(GD) proteases compared to wild-type BoNT/X and X(PC) variants but also uncovered a potential exosite interaction conserved from wild-type BoNT/X and retained in evolved gasdermin D-cleaving variants.

Cell death in cancer cell lines To evaluate the ability of leading candidate proteases to induce cell death via procaspase-1 and gasdermin D cleavage, we stably integrated X(PC) and X(GD), as well as catalytically inactive variants as negative controls, into cancer cell lines under doxycycline-induced expression (Fig. 5a). After 24 h of induction, cells were stained with Annexin V and 7-AAD to assess cell death phenotypes. Annexin V binds phosphatidylserines that translocate to the outer leaflet of the membrane during early apoptosis61, whereas 7-AAD is a membrane-impermeable DNA dye

that labels cells with compromised membrane integrity, identifying cells undergoing lytic forms of cell death such as necrosis, secondary necrosis and pyroptosis62,63. For the purposes of this study, we define 7-AAD+ cells as undergoing lytic cell death. While this lytic population likely includes pyroptosis in contexts where caspase-1 and/or gasdermin D are expressed, multiple lytic pathways may be engaged. Thus, Annexin V+7-AAD⁻ cells represent apoptotic populations, while Annexin V+7-AAD+ cells reflect lytic cell death including pyroptotic death (Fig. 5a). We first examined cell death in THP-1 cells, a monocytic leukemia line that expresses both caspase-1 and gasdermin D. Following induction, X(PC) triggered concurrent apoptotic and lytic cell death, suggesting that its activity extends beyond direct cleavage of procaspase-1 (Fig. 5b). This simultaneous engagement of multiple death execution programs, spanning both apoptotic and highly inflammatory lytic mechanisms, shares biochemical hallmarks with PANoptosis64. To dissect the role of caspases in the observed profile, we included two inhibitors: Q-VD-OPh (referred to hereafter as QVD), a pan-caspase inhibitor targeting caspases 1, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12, and Ac-DEVD-CHO (referred to hereafter as DEVD), which selectively inhibits caspases 3, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Although QVD inhibits caspase-1, it did not fully suppress 7-AAD+ lytic death in our assays. In THP-1 cells expressing X(PC), QVD treatment reduced lytic death by approximately 33%, suggesting partial caspase-1 dependence (Fig. 5b). Given that we also demonstrated that X(PC) cleaves multiple downstream caspase substrates, this partial reduction could result from engagement of alternate caspase-mediated pathways or off-target cleavage of other protease-sensitive death effectors. It is also possible that as QVD substantially reduces apoptosis in X(PC) lines, the reduction of lytic death is consequently decreased due to loss of secondary necrosis. To further evaluate whether QVD inhibits caspase-1-driven death in this system, we used a control THP-1 line with doxycycline-inducible, active caspase-1. Following induction, QVD reduced lytic death by only 23% (Extended Data Fig. 9a). As an additional positive control, we also integrated and expressed a truncated Bid protein that induces apoptosis65 and observed that QVD reduces apoptotic death by almost 50% (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Because caspase-1 directly cleaves gasdermin D to drive pyroptosis, these results suggest that QVD does not fully block caspase-1 activity under these conditions. One possible explanation is that low levels of caspase-1 activity are sufficient to initiate a cascade leading to lytic death, and once gasdermin D is cleaved, downstream pore formation proceeds independently of caspase activity. Alternatively, leaky X(PC) expression before full QVD inhibition may allow enough early cleavage to trigger cell death. To further confirm the cells were dying in a lytic manner, we also imaged THP-1 cell lines induced to express X(PC) with 0.5 µg ml−1 doxycycline for 12 h every 10 min. Cell death was morphologically consistent with lytic death, characterized by rapid loss of membrane integrity and subsequent 7-AAD uptake without the cell shrinkage typically associated with apoptosis

(Extended Data Fig. 9b and Supplementary Video 1). Together, these findings suggest that X(PC) triggers a caspase-1-dependent lytic cascade, but that this pathway is only partially sensitive to QVD inhibition likely due to the threshold-like nature of pyroptotic signaling, and that off-target cleavage of proteins such as the substrates uncovered during profiling contributes to this complex, PANoptotic-like cell death. Apoptotic activity induced by X(PC) was substantially reduced ~97% by QVD but not by DEVD, suggesting involvement of caspases not targeted by DEVD, such as caspase-9 or caspase-12 (Fig. 5b). To further investigate this possibility, we transfected HEK293T cells with MYC-tagged, full-length caspases 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12 and incubated their cell lysates with purified X(PC) or BoNT/X protease (Extended Data Fig. 9c). As with previous caspase-1 assays, each caspase was rendered catalytically inactive to prevent toxicity during expression. We found that X(PC) cleaved caspase-9, but the cleavage product was inconsistent with canonical activation events at Asp 315 or Asp 330. Notably, caspase-9 was not identified in our substrate screen, and the cleavage region lacks a recognizable motif, suggesting that this site may not have been represented in the substrate library. Further studies are needed to determine whether X(PC) directly cleaves and activates caspase-9. In contrast to X(PC), X(GD) exclusively induced lytic cell death in THP-1 cells, consistent with gasdermin D cleavage (Fig. 5b). This death was not inhibited by QVD or DEVD, supporting a caspase-independent mechanism. Importantly, wild-type BoNT/X protease did not induce notable apoptotic or lytic cell death (Extended Data Fig. 9a). These results support a model in which procaspase-1-cleaving X(PC) activates multiple cell death pathways, including both apoptotic and lytic programs, whereas gasdermin D-cleaving X(GD) acts through a more selective lytic mechanism. We further evaluated X(PC5)a and X(PC5)b in lentivirally integrated THP-1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Although these proteases retained the ability to cleave procaspase-1 in co-transfected HEK293T cells, albeit at a reduced capacity compared to X(PC), their activity was substantially diminished in the THP-1 system. These findings further suggest that an additional round of negative selection against IL-1β reduced the stability of these proteases, making them ineffective at initiating cell death. Next, we tested whether lentivirus integrated proteases could trigger death in non-hematopoietic cancer lines, including Jurkat (T cell leukemia) and U2OS (osteosarcoma) cells (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f). Although all three lines demonstrate measurable gasdermin D transcript expression (based on Human Protein Atlas (HPA) transcriptome data), X(GD) did not robustly induce cell death in any of them. This observation suggests that additional regulatory mechanisms, such as post-translational modification, may be required for gasdermin D-mediated cell death in these contexts66–68. A negligible fraction of cells were propidium iodide+ alone, indicating that X(PC) does not merely initiate unprogrammed necrotic cell death in SUP-B15 cells but rather directly activates a pyroptotic lytic death through caspase activation. By comparison, uninduced X(PC) SUP-B15 cell lines and wild-type SUP-B15 cells exhibited approximately 10% FAM-FLICA positivity, suggesting basal pyroptotic caspase activation (Fig. 5d), but X(PC) activity drastically amplifies this activation to execute pyroptotic death. Overall, we demonstrated that X(PC) and X(GD) selectively initiate targeted cell death. For X(PC), we demonstrated that this cell death is driven by the direct activation of caspase-1 in SUP-B15 cells, successfully mimicking canonical pyroptosis. However, as revealed by our global profiling and the mixed cell death phenotypes observed in other cell lines, X(PC) also possesses the capability to engage broader, multipathway networks, such as caspase-dependent apoptosis.

Self-delivery of evolved proteases into cancer cells To harness the self-delivery capabilities of BoNT proteases, we expressed and purified evolved proteases X(PC) and X(GD) as fusions with the wild-type BoNT/X translocation domain (HN). No readily available neuronal cancer cell line expressed both caspase-1 and gasdermin D at appreciable levels based on RNA expression data from the HPA. As a result, we could not use the native HC domain to mediate receptor binding. Instead, we relied on prior findings showing that BoNT proteases can be delivered to cells in culture independently of the HC domain69 (Fig. 5e). Notably, the BoNT/X HN domain has been shown to effectively deliver a range of protein cargos with minimal toxicity28. Indeed, several clinically relevant engineered BoNTs, such as targeted secretion inhibitors, omit the HC domain entirely and retain efficacy70,71. X(PC)-HN induced potent cell death in SUP-B15 cancer cells, while catalytically inactive X(PC)-HN and X(PC) protease alone had no effect (Fig. 5f). X(GD) also induced cell death, although less potently (Fig. 5g). Importantly, neither protease exhibited toxicity in HEK293T cells (Fig. 5f,g), indicating cell-type selectivity that preferentially kills SUP-B15 cells. These data represent the first demonstration

of self-delivery of an evolved BoNT protease targeting a non-SNARE substrate in cancer cells. To evaluate the anticancer activity of self-delivering X(PC) across diverse genetic backgrounds, we conducted a pooled viability screen of 475 barcoded human cancer cell lines using the PRISM platform72. This screen enabled us to examine protease efficacy on cells from diverse tumor types, including solid tumors. The cell line pool was treated with X(PC) at five concentrations (2, 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 µM) in triplicate for 24 h (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Following cell lysis and barcode sequencing, viability was quantified as the log2FC in abundance relative to untreated controls. To establish a rigorous threshold for X(PC) sensitivity amidst the inherent variance of high-throughput pooled screening, we applied the following criteria: cell lines were classified as sensitive (‘hits’) if they exhibited a significant (P < 0.05) log2(fold de-enrichment) of ≤–0.5 in at least one of the three highest doses (0.5, 1 and 2 µM; Extended Data Fig. 10b,c and Supplementary Tables 9 and 10). Furthermore, hit nomination required a negative dose–response slope (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d and Supplementary Table 10). This filtering identified 20 sensitive cell lines, notably including five lines derived from the central nervous system, suggesting potential susceptibility within specific solid tumor niches (Extended Data Fig. 10b). To identify transcriptomic biomarkers predictive of X(PC) sensitivity, we cross-referenced our PRISM de-enrichment data with basal RNA-sequencing expression profiles from the HPA. We compared the transcriptomes of the protease-sensitive lines against the 29 most highly resistant lines. Resistant lines were defined as all cell lines that had positive log2 (fold enrichment) and nonsignificant P values at the top two doses. Gene expression, quantified as transcripts per million (TPM), was transformed with a pseudocount of 1 (log2(TPM + 1)) to compress the dynamic range and stabilize variance for downstream analysis. To evaluate the statistical significance of these transcriptomic differences, we applied an unpaired Welch’s t-test. Differential expression analysis revealed caspase-1 as a top-tier biomarker of protease sensitivity, ranking 10th of 13,339 transcripts by integrated rank score (– log10P × log2FC; Supplementary Table 11). Filtering for stringent enrichment (Welch’s P < 0.05, log2FC > 0.5) yielded a signature of 84 genes significantly upregulated in sensitive lines (Extended Data Fig. 10e and Supplementary Table 12). Within this signature, caspase-1 emerged as a top-tier biomarker of protease sensitivity (log2 (fold change) = 1.28, P = 0.024; Extended Data Fig. 10f), alongside other key inflammasome and immune regulators like NLRC5 and caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 16 (Supplementary Table 12). To systematically evaluate the pathways driving this sensitivity, we performed continuous gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) ranking all mapped genes by their Pearson correlation coefficient (R) between basal expression (log2(TPM + 1)) and the PRISM log2(fold de-enrichment) across the 470 matched cell lines (note that 5 cell lines were not listed on HPA and were therefore not included; Supplemental Table 13). Proliferation signatures (for example, E2F targets, MYC targets and G2M checkpoint targets) were the dominant predictors of X(PC) sensitivity. This observation likely reflects the escalated endocytosis required for cellular uptake or the assay kinetics of rapidly dividing populations yielding more pronounced viability fold changes. However, innate immune activation also appeared as a dominant signature, specifically interferon-α (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.001) and interferon-γ (FDR = 0.005) responses. Notably, these immune signatures were driven by the core enrichment of transcripts from our 84-biomarker panel, including NLRC5, indicating a baseline proinflammatory state in X(PC)-sensitive cells. Specific mechanistic analysis using the C2 Reactome database mirrored these findings. Global enrichment was dominated by cell cycle and mRNA splicing pathways, reinforcing the prerequisite of high proliferation. The Reactome analysis also captured the baseline inflammatory state via high-ranking viral infection signatures (for example,

Notably, this database also identified pyroptosis (normalized enrichment score = –1.57, FDR = 0.036) and defective pyroptosis (normalized enrichment score = –1.59, FDR = 0.029) gene sets as significantly enriched in X(PC)-sensitive cells. Collectively, these high-throughput screening data suggest that evolved BoNT proteases can self-deliver across diverse cancer lineages, potentially targeting highly proliferative, immune-primed cells. Future studies will need to individually evaluate these nominated hit cell lines to confirm their true susceptibility to X(PC)-mediated killing.

X(PC) kills drug-resistant KPCY tumor cells in vitro and in vivo To evaluate the antitumor potential of X(PC) in a highly recalcitrant solid tumor model, we used the KPCY 6419c5 mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cell line73. Derived from the autochthonous (KPC) mouse model, this clonal line represents an immunologically ‘cold’ tumor microenvironment characterized by low T cell infiltration and profound resistance to GAFCP, an aggressive combination chemoimmunotherapy regimen consisting of gemcitabine, nab-paclitaxel, anti-CD40 agonist, anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1. We engineered KPCY 6419c5 cells to stably harbor a doxycycline-inducible X(PC) construct. Following doxycycline induction in vitro, we observed potent cytotoxicity, with over 20% of the cellular population undergoing lytic cell death (Fig. 6a). Furthermore, this activity was specific to X(PC), as wild-type BoNT/X failed to induce lytic death above background levels (Fig. 6a). Although the precise molecular mechanism driving cell death in these cultured engineered KPCY cells remains to be elucidated, we confirmed that X(PC) successfully cleaves mouse caspase-1 between Glu 312 and Asp 313, a position adjacent to the native Asp 308 autoproteolysis site (Fig. 6b). This finding suggests that a conserved caspase-1-associated, multipathway death program may be contributing to the observed cytotoxicity. We also confirmed that KPCY 6419c5 cells express mouse caspase-1 by using real-time quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR; average cycling threshold (Ct) = 31.3 for Casp1 compared to 18.6 for Gapdh). Comparatively, X(PC) induction did not induce cell death in the mouse melanoma cell line B16-F10, which lacks caspase-1 expression74 (Supplementary Fig. 8).

To assess in vivo efficacy, we engrafted these doxycycline-inducible KPCY cells into syngeneic mice and monitored tumor volume over a 32-day period. Doxycycline administration on days 7 and 13 after engraftment induced in vivo X(PC) expression, resulting in a highly significant reduction in tumor volume (P < 0.0001) at the final two time points (days 27 and 32) compared to untreated controls (Fig. 6c). Notably, this robust tumor growth inhibition was achieved in a model in which GAFCP combination therapy does not inhibit tumor growth73. Together, these data provide in vivo proof of concept that evolved BoNT proteases can effectively eliminate drug-resistant solid tumors, providing a foundation for future systemic delivery applications using modified receptor-binding domains to actively target the protease to malignant tissues.

Discussion Proteases are key modulators of cell state, uniquely capable of driving irreversible biological transitions by cleaving specific protein targets. Their catalytic activity enables rapid remodeling of cellular pathways, and their substrate specificity offers a route to precisely rewire signaling networks. Despite these advantages, therapeutic proteases, including all currently approved BoNT drugs26, remain limited in scope, with most clinical applications relying on native enzymes acting on endogenous substrates20. Expanding their use requires the ability to reprogram protease specificity to cleave targets with functional consequences for cell fate. Here we advance and apply a generalizable system for evolving programmable proteases using BoNT/X protease and PACE. Focusing on cell death, a process tightly governed by proteolysis, we evolved proteases capable of initiating lytic cell death. The evolved BoNT/X proteases cleave either procaspase-1 or gasdermin D, driving potent cytotoxicity in cancer cells. These proteases function as self-delivering agents when reconstituted with the BoNT translocation domain, enabling intracellular activity without the need for additional delivery vectors. Notably, X(PC) and X(GD) exhibit distinct cell death phenotypes and kinetic profiles, demonstrating that evolved proteases can drive different outcomes depending on their chosen target and

biochemical properties. Whereas X(GD) mediates an exclusively lytic execution program, X(PC) initiates concurrent lytic and apoptotic cell death. Although we confirmed that X(PC) successfully drives pyroptosis through direct caspase activation in specific contexts such as SUP-B15 cells, canonical pyroptosis is a highly regulated process that often requires multiple coordinated signals. The resistance or mixed cell death phenotypes observed in other target-expressing cell lines likely reflect an absence of these requisite contextual signals. In such environments, the broader substrate reactivity of X(PC) overcomes this biological bottleneck by triggering a complex cell death program consistent with PANoptosis, rather than isolated canonical cleavage events. To understand evolved protease substrate specificity more comprehensively, we developed a substrate compatibility profiling system that maps substrate preferences and nominates potential off-target substrates across the human proteome. We anticipate that this tool will prove useful for both therapeutic design and understanding on-target versus off-target effects in reprogrammed proteases. Notably, although X(PC) targets many proteins within caspasedriven pathways, it often cleaves them at noncanonical sites. For example, X(PC) cleaves the inflammatory cytokine pro-IL-1β between Glu 18 and Asp 19, distinct from the canonical caspase-1 sites at Asp 26 and Asp 116. Similarly, X(PC) cleaves ATG3 and numerous other caspase substrates identified in the MerCASBA database within 30 amino acids of their native cleavage sites. This noncanonical processing may either mimic caspase activity or yield unintended consequences by destroying effector domains or native caspase motifs. An important next step toward enhancing the specificity of these evolved proteases is characterizing the cleavage fragments of off-target substrates and further rounds of negative selection against relevant off-targets. Although our initial substrate profiling and TMT-TAILS data provide a foundation for understanding the specificity of variants like X(PC), defining their therapeutic relevance will require additional safety assessments. Future studies comparing the global off-target and toxicity profiles of these self-delivering proteases head-to-head with established small-molecule inducers of pyroptosis and apoptosis will help inform their therapeutic potential. Our findings also highlight a specificity–activity trade-off during directed evolution. While stringent negative selection yielded the highly specific X(PC5) variants, it simultaneously attenuated their expression, stability and overall cleavage efficiency in mammalian cells. Although the current catalytic efficiency of X(PC) is sufficient to slow tumor growth in vivo in the highly treatment-resistant KPCY model, advancing these enzymes for broader systemic use will require overcoming this evolutionary bottleneck to maximize both potency and selectivity. Future optimization paths may benefit from integrating artificial intelligence-driven computational protein design to reinforce the BoNT protease scaffold75. A more stable scaffold would better tolerate the structurally disruptive mutations often required for substrate recognition and may allow simultaneous access to variants with both the high selectivity seen in the X(PC5) series and the robust intracellular activity of X(PC). Although we achieved effective protease activity and self-delivery in cancer cells in cell culture, BoNT holotoxins are naturally restricted to neuronal targeting due to the specificities of their receptor-binding domains. Overcoming this limitation will be critical to fully realizing the potential of BoNT-delivered proteases for in vivo applications. In this study, we established in vivo efficacy through a doxycycline-inducible X(PC) cell line. Recent advances have demonstrated the feasibility of replacing BoNT receptor-binding domains with nanobodies to redirect specificity toward cancer-relevant surface markers, although the efficiency of such an architecture has not been confirmed in vivo30. We envision further improvements through directed evolution of the receptor-binding domain to recognize additional receptors or tumor-specific antigens. Advancements in targeted delivery could

also mitigate systemic toxicity that may result from off-target protease cleavage. Together, our findings establish a versatile strategy for evolving proteases that cleave non-native, therapeutically relevant targets and reprogram cellular behavior. By leveraging cell death as a model system, we show that engineered proteases can function as bespoke effectors of cell fate, providing a foundation for programmable catalytic biological therapeutics.

Methods Cloning and plasmid preparation Gibson cloning using NEBuilder HiFi DNA Assembly (New England Biolabs) or USER cloning (New England Biolabs) was used to construct all plasmids. Primers were either taken from previous studies23 or ordered through Integrated DNA Technologies. All PCR reactions were performed using Phusion HiFi polymerase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with nuclease-free water (Qiagen). For other applications, water was purified using a Milli-Q purification system (Millipore). Following Gibson or USER assembly, products were transformed into Mach1 chemically competent E. coli (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Selection antibiotics were used at the following final concentrations: 100 μg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 μg ml−1 spectinomycin, 50 μg ml−1 kanamycin, 25 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol and 10 μg ml−1 tetracycline. Plasmid DNA was amplified using the Illustra TempliPhi 100 Amplification Kit (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) before Sanger or Nanopore sequencing (Quintara Biosciences). Sequence-confirmed plasmids were purified using either the Miniprep Kit or the Plasmid Plus Midi Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Plasmid concentrations were measured using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. A complete list of primers and plasmids can be found in Supplementary Tables 8 and 14.

Preparation and transformation of chemically competent cells Strain S2060 was used for all luciferase, PANCE and PACE experiments. To prepare competent cells, an overnight culture was diluted 1:100 into 50 ml of 2× YT medium (United States Biological) supplemented with tetracycline and grown at 37 °C with shaking at 220 rpm until the OD600 reached 0.4–0.6. Cultures were chilled on ice for 10 min, pelleted by centrifugation at 4,000g for 10 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 5 ml of chilled TSS (LB medium supplemented with 5% (vol/vol) DMSO, 10% (wt/vol) PEG 3350 and 20 mM MgCl2). Cells were mixed gently and aliquoted into 100-μl volumes. If not being used immediately, aliquots were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until use. For transformation, 100 μl of fresh or thawed competent cells was combined with 1–2 μl of plasmid DNA (up to three plasmids per transformation), 20 μl of 5× KCM buffer (500 mM KCl, 150 mM CaCl2 and 250 mM MgCl2) and water to a final volume of 100 μl. The mixture was incubated on ice for 15 min, heat shocked at 42 °C for 75 s and recovered in 500 μl of SOC medium (New England Biolabs) for 1–1.5 h at 37 °C with shaking at 220 rpm. Transformed cells were plated on 2× YT agar plates containing the appropriate antibiotics and incubated overnight at 37 °C.

Preparation and transformation of electrocompetent cells S2060 E. coli cells containing pJC175e were grown in Davis Rich Medium (DRM) to late log phase (OD600 = 0.7–0.9). Five milliliters of culture was used per 50-μl electroporation, and four to six electroporations were typically sufficient for 1,000-fold coverage of a 30,000-member library. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 3,000g for 12 min at 4 °C and washed with 10 ml of ice-cold Milli-Q water. Next, 10 ml of ice-cold density buffer (20% (wt/vol) glycerol, 1.5% mannitol) was gently added to the bottom of the tube. Cells were centrifuged for 25 min at 2,750g and 4 °C in a swing-out rotor (acceleration/deceleration set to 4). The top aqueous layer was carefully removed, and any residual buffer was removed with a P1000 pipette. Pellets were resuspended in density buffer (50 μl per electroporation). For electroporation, 3 μl of DNA was added to 50 μl of electrocompetent cells, transferred to a prechilled 1-mm gap electroporation cuvette and pulsed at 1,800 V, 200 Ω, 25 μF. Cells were immediately recovered in 10 ml of 2× YT, incubated at 37 °C with shaking for 10–15 min and plated at appropriate dilutions.

Bacteriophage cloning For USER or Gibson assembly of phage, 10 pmol of each PCR fragment (with 0.5 pmol of DpnI-digested backbone, if used) was added to a final

volume of 10 μl. After assembly, the 10-μl reaction was transformed into 100 μl of chemically competent S2060 E. coli cells containing pJC175e. The pJC175e plasmid enables activity-independent phage propagation. Following heat shock (75 s at 42 °C), cells were placed on ice for 2 min and grown in antibiotic-free 2× YT medium for 5 h at 37 °C with shaking. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 10,000g for 1 min, and individual plaques were isolated and grown in DRM for 6–8 h. Bacteria were removed by centrifugation at 6,000g for 10 min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22-μm PVDF centrifugal filter (Millipore). Phage DNA was sequenced by Nanopore (Quintara Biosciences), and sequence-confirmed phage were stored at 4 °C.

Plaque assays Phage were plaqued on S2060 E. coli host cells containing the pJC175e plasmid. Host cells were grown from an overnight culture by diluting 1:50 into DRM supplemented with the appropriate antibiotics and incubated at 37 °C until the OD600 reached 0.8–1.0 (~3 h). Cultures were then placed on ice while phage samples were prepared. Phage stocks were serially diluted in DRM by 10-fold increments, up to 106-fold. For plate preparation, melted 2× YT agar (1.5%, 55 °C) was mixed with Bluo-gal (Gold Biotechnology, 10% (wt/vol) in DMSO) to a final concentration of 0.05%, pipetted into quadrants of quartered Petri dishes (2 ml per quadrant) and allowed to solidify at room temperature for 5 min. Top agar was prepared as a 2:1 mixture of 2× YT medium and melted 2× YT agar (1.5%), yielding a final agar concentration of 0.6%, and held at 55 °C until use. For each phage dilution, 100 μl of host cells was mixed with 10 μl of phage in 2-ml library tubes (VWR International). Then, 900 μl of top agar was added, mixed by pipetting and immediately poured onto a solidified quadrant of the Petri dish. Top agar was allowed to solidify undisturbed for 2 min at 25 °C. Plates were incubated at 37 °C overnight without inversion. Phage titers were determined by counting blue plaques. For higher-throughput assays, 24-well plates were used with adjusted volumes: 1 ml of bottom agar, 300 μl of top agar, 10 μl of phage and 50 μl of host cells per well.

General method for PACE PACE experiments were performed using previously described apparatuses and protocols, including host strains, lagoons, chemostats and media27. Chemically competent S2060 cells were transformed with accessory plasmid(s) and the mutagenesis plasmid MP6 and plated on 2× YT agar containing 1.5% agar, 100 mM glucose (to repress mutagenesis) and the appropriate antibiotics. Twelve colonies were picked into individual wells of a 96-well plate containing 1 ml of DRM with the appropriate antibiotics. Cultures were serially diluted tenfold across eight wells, sealed with porous film and incubated at 37 °C with shaking (220 rpm) for 16–18 h. Wells with OD600 values between 0.3 and 0.4 were pooled to inoculate a 100-ml chemostat containing DRM. The chemostat was grown to an OD600 of 0.4–0.8 and continuously diluted with fresh DRM at a rate of 1.0–1.5 volumes per h to maintain a steady-state culture at a volume of 80–100 ml. Lagoons were inoculated with 100 μl of filtered phage stock at titers between 107 and 1010 plaque-forming units per ml or with pooled phage from a previous PACE endpoint. For mixed-host experiments, lagoons received equal flow from two chemostats, each bearing different accessory plasmids, for 24 h. At designated time points, 1-ml samples were collected from lagoon waste lines and centrifuged at 8,000g for 2 min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22-μm PVDF centrifugal filter (Millipore) and stored at 4 °C. Phage titers were determined by plaque assays using S2060 cells with pJC175e. For sequencing, individual plaques were picked and subjected to rolling circle amplification before Nanopore sequencing. PANCE PANCE experiments were performed according to established protocols. Between four and eight colonies were picked into individual wells of a 96-well plate containing 1 ml of DRM supplemented with antibiotics. Wells with OD600 values between 0.3 and 0.4 were pooled, treated with 20 mM arabinose to induce mutagenesis and distributed into the desired number of 1-ml cultures in a 96-well plate.
